section.title: The Call of Samuel
section.sectionRationale: In a time when the word of the LORD was rare, God speaks. He calls the boy Samuel by name in the night, three times, until Eli understands and teaches him to answer. The LORD entrusts Samuel with a hard word confirming the doom of Eli's house, and Samuel, though afraid, tells it all. From then on the LORD is with him, letting none of his words fall to the ground, and all Israel knows Samuel is confirmed as a prophet. It is one movement: God raises up His prophet and His word returns to Israel.
section.thesis: When God's word had grown scarce and Israel's lamps were nearly out, the LORD calls a listening boy by name, gives him His word even when it is heavy, and establishes him as a trustworthy prophet, so that the God who had fallen silent begins again to speak and to lead His people.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the scarce word and the sleeping sanctuary, verses 1 to 3; the threefold call and Samuel's answer, verses 4 to 10; the word of judgment on Eli's house, verses 11 to 14; and Samuel telling all and being confirmed as prophet, verses 15 to 21.

units.label: The scarce word and the sleeping sanctuary
units.note: the word of the LORD was rare

verses.text: And the boy Samuel ministered to the LORD before Eli. Now in those days the {{dabar|word of the LORD}} was rare, and visions were scarce.
And at that time Eli, whose eyesight had grown so dim that he could not see, was lying in his room.
Before the lamp of God had gone out, Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was located.

units.label: The threefold call and Samuel's answer
units.note: Speak, for Your servant is listening

verses.text: Then the LORD called to Samuel, and he answered, “Here I am.”
He ran to Eli and said, “Here I am, for you have called me.” “I did not call,” Eli replied. “Go back and lie down.” So he went and lay down.
Once again the LORD called, “Samuel!” So Samuel got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am, for you have called me.” “My son, I did not call,” Eli replied. “Go back and lie down.”
Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, because the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him.
Once again, for the third time, the LORD called to Samuel. He got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am, for you have called me.” Then Eli realized that it was the LORD who was calling the boy.
“Go and lie down,” he said to Samuel, “and if He calls you, say, ‘Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening.’” So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
Then the LORD came and stood there, calling as before, “Samuel! Samuel!” And Samuel answered, “Speak, for Your servant is {{shama|listening}}.”

units.label: The word of judgment on Eli's house
units.note: the ears of all who hear it will tingle

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Samuel, “I am about to do something in Israel at which the ears of all who hear it will tingle.
On that day I will carry out against Eli everything I have spoken about his house, from beginning to end.
I told him that I would judge his house forever for the iniquity of which he knows, because his sons blasphemed God and he did not restrain them.
Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli, ‘The iniquity of Eli’s house shall never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering.’”

units.label: Samuel confirmed as prophet
units.note: the LORD let none of his words fall to the ground

verses.text: Samuel lay down until the morning; then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. He was afraid to tell Eli the vision,
but Eli called to him and said, “Samuel, my son.” “Here I am,” answered Samuel.
“What was the message He gave you?” Eli asked. “Do not hide it from me. May God punish you, and ever so severely, if you hide from me anything He said to you.”
So Samuel told him everything and did not hide a thing from him. “He is the LORD,” replied Eli. “Let Him do what is good in His eyes.”
And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him, and He let none of Samuel’s words fall to the ground.
So all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was confirmed as a {{navi|prophet}} of the LORD.
And the LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, because there He revealed Himself to Samuel by His word.

dabar.gloss: Word, matter, thing spoken. The chapter opens and closes with the word of the LORD: rare at the start, revealed to Samuel at the end. In the Old Testament God's word is never mere information; it is His living speech that judges, saves, and comes to pass, the very thing Israel had been starved of.

shama.gloss: To hear, listen, obey. Eli teaches Samuel to answer, Your servant is listening, and true hearing in Hebrew always leans toward obeying. Samuel's readiness to hear stands against Eli's sons, who would not listen, and models the posture God seeks from His people, faith that comes by hearing.

navi.gloss: Prophet, one who speaks for God. A prophet does not invent his message but delivers the word entrusted to him. Samuel is confirmed as a navi because the LORD lets none of his words fall to the ground; he becomes the first of the great prophets, the mouth through whom God will raise up king and kingdom.

basic.context: Israel is in a spiritual famine: the word of the LORD is rare, visions are few, and even Eli the priest is going blind, a picture of the whole nation's dimness. Then one night God calls the boy Samuel by name. Samuel does not yet know the LORD's voice and keeps running to Eli, until Eli realizes God is calling and teaches him to answer, Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening. God gives Samuel a hard first message, the certain judgment of Eli's house. Though afraid, Samuel tells Eli everything, and Eli bows to God's will. From then on God is with Samuel, and all Israel knows he is a true prophet. The question is: will God speak again to a people who have stopped listening? He will, through a boy who listens.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative about how God raised up His prophet, not a template promising everyone a dramatic night-time call. Its enduring truths are that God takes the initiative to speak, that hearing God rightly means being ready to obey even hard words, and that a true prophet is known by words that come true. We should not reduce it to a devotional about listening, though listening is real; it is about God restoring His word to Israel through Samuel.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter is framed by the dabar, the word of the LORD, rare at the start and revealed to Samuel at the end. Eli teaches the boy to say, Your servant is shama, listening, and in Hebrew to hear is to lean toward obeying. By the close, Samuel is confirmed as a navi, a prophet, because God lets none of his words fall to the ground.
basic.typology: Samuel, the prophet raised up when God's word was scarce and confirmed because his words never fail, points forward to the Prophet greater than Samuel, Jesus, the very Word of God made flesh. The listening servant who receives and faithfully delivers God's word foreshadows the perfect Servant who speaks only what the Father gives Him.
basic.christ: Samuel is the first in the great line of prophets that runs to John the Baptist and finds its end in Christ, the Prophet like Moses whom God promised to raise up, whom we must hear. Where Samuel received the word, Jesus is the Word, God's final and full speech to us. And where Samuel spoke a word of unatonable judgment on Eli's house, Christ becomes the atonement no sacrifice at Shiloh could provide, the mediator of a better word.
basic.god: God is the God who speaks and who takes the initiative; He calls Samuel before Samuel knows Him. He is patient, calling again and again until the boy is ready. He is holy and just, keeping His sworn word of judgment against a house that despised Him. And He is faithful to His people, refusing to leave them without His word, raising up a prophet so that His voice is heard from Dan to Beersheba.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 18 promises a prophet like Moses whom the people must heed. Hebrews 1 says God has now spoken by His Son. Amos 3 says the Lord does nothing without revealing it to His prophets. And 1 Samuel 2 gives the earlier word against Eli that this chapter confirms.
basic.oneStory: In a silent age God speaks again, raising up Samuel as His prophet. Through Samuel God will anoint Saul and David and carry His purposes toward the promised King. The God who speaks here will keep speaking through the prophets until He speaks at last by His Son, the living Word who saves.

context.literary: The threefold call is a recognized call type-scene in Hebrew narrative, most famously heard in the doubled naming at Abraham's binding of Isaac, Abraham, Abraham, and Moses' burning bush, Moses, Moses; each repetition builds tension and marks the moment as unmistakably significant rather than an accident of hearing. Here the pattern is stretched to four callings in all, since Eli's coaching in verse 9 sits between the third and fourth, so the narrator can show not only God's persistence but a boy's growing readiness to answer rightly. The chapter is framed by an inclusio on the word dabar, God's word: rare and scarce at the opening, verse 1, but filling the whole land by the closing verses, so the very structure of the passage enacts the change it describes, moving from famine to abundance of divine speech. The narrator also exploits dramatic irony throughout the middle section: the reader is told from the first sentence that the LORD is calling, while Samuel and even Eli remain in the dark for several rounds, so that the audience watches a boy misread God's voice as his mentor's for far longer than a modern reader expects, heightening both the humor and the pathos of verse 7's blunt aside, Samuel did not yet know the LORD. The chapter's final movement, from a private nighttime exchange to a public, nationwide recognition of Samuel as a confirmed prophet, deliberately widens the lens from one boy's bed to the whole territory from Dan to Beersheba, turning a domestic scene into a national turning point.
context.historical: Israel's sanctuary lamp, described in Exodus 27:20-21 and Leviticus 24:2-4, was to be kept burning from evening until morning on pure oil, so the detail that Samuel lay down before the lamp of God had gone out places the scene believably in the last hours of night, just before dawn, when a junior attendant like Samuel might have been sleeping within call of the sanctuary precincts near the ark, ready to relight or tend the lamp if needed. Across the ancient Near East, kings and priests regularly sought a divine word through professional diviners, dream interpreters, and omen readers, methods that treated the god's will as something to be extracted by technique. Israel's law rejected that whole apparatus, Deuteronomy 18:9-14, and offered instead a single, simple test for any Israelite claiming to speak for God: does what he says come true, Deuteronomy 18:21-22. This chapter shows that test being met in real time, so that Samuel's authority as a prophet rests not on any technique he mastered but on the plain fact that the LORD let none of his words fall to the ground. The set phrase from Dan to Beersheba, naming Israel's northernmost and southernmost settled points, was a standard way of saying the whole land, used throughout Judges, Samuel, and Kings; its appearance here signals that Samuel's recognition was not confined to Shiloh's household but became common knowledge across the entire tribal territory, a rare and public vindication for so young a figure.
context.canonical: Samuel's night in the sanctuary opens a distinct pattern of prophetic call narratives that recurs through the rest of the Old Testament: Isaiah likewise receives his commission inside the sanctuary, seeing the LORD high and lifted up in the temple, Isaiah 6:1-8, and Jeremiah, like Samuel a very young man, at first protests his own unreadiness, saying, I am only a boy, before God overrules his hesitation and puts words in his mouth, Jeremiah 1:4-10. Each of these accounts shares Samuel's basic shape: an unlikely or unready messenger, a setting close to God's own dwelling, and language given rather than invented. The chapter's closing claim, that the LORD let none of Samuel's words fall to the ground, becomes a kind of watchword the rest of Scripture keeps testing and confirming; centuries later Solomon can declare in his temple dedication prayer that not one word has failed of all the LORD's good promise, 1 Kings 8:56, the identical confidence Samuel's ministry first established as a live pattern for Israel's leaders. Isaiah later generalizes the same principle into a description of God's word altogether, that it will not return to Him empty but will accomplish the purpose for which He sent it, Isaiah 55:11, turning what began as a specific comment about one prophet's reliability into a settled doctrine of how all divine speech behaves. The oracle Samuel delivers against Eli, moreover, explicitly reaches back to confirm the earlier word already given through the unnamed man of God in chapter 2, showing the canon's own habit of having later revelation authenticate and deepen earlier revelation rather than replace it.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The author is doing more here than reporting a childhood memory; he is establishing Samuel's credentials for every major decision Samuel will make later in the book, anointing Saul, rejecting Saul, anointing David in Saul's place. A reader who has watched this chapter unfold already knows, before any of those later controversial acts, that Samuel is not a self-appointed political operator but a man whose every word the LORD has personally guaranteed. The writer also wants his audience to see how God can still use a compromised leader instrumentally even while judging him; Eli, under sentence himself, is nonetheless the one who correctly interprets what is happening and teaches Samuel how to answer, showing that God's ordinary means of raising up new leadership can run through flawed old leadership on its way out, without either excusing that leadership's failures or discarding its remaining usefulness. Finally, by lingering over Samuel's fear and reluctance to report the hard word to Eli, the author models for future readers, especially future prophets and truth tellers, that faithful speech does not require confidence, only obedience even through fear.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter describes one unrepeatable, God-initiated call to establish Israel's next prophet; it does not prescribe an audible voice in the night as the normal way anyone discovers God's calling on their life. The New Testament ordinarily directs believers to Scripture already given, the Spirit's inward witness, and the wisdom of the gathered church rather than a fresh nighttime summons, and building an expectation of literal voices from this single narrative risks both disappointment and confusion for sincere readers. Eli's submission in verse 18, He is the LORD, let Him do what is good in His eyes, models a right posture toward a settled, already announced divine judgment on his own house, not a general command to accept every hardship passively without protest or action; Scripture elsewhere commends resisting injustice and pleading with God against suffering, so Eli's words describe fitting submission to a specific, already declared sentence rather than prescribing fatalism as a universal response to every difficulty.

debates.question: Why does God repeat the judgment on Eli's house already spoken in chapter 2?

views.label: To confirm and personally commission it through Samuel
views.case: The word first came by an unnamed man of God; now it is given directly to Samuel, establishing him as the prophet who carries God's word and confirming the certainty of the judgment by a second, weightier witness.

views.label: To underline the finality of the sentence
views.case: The added oath, that Eli's iniquity will never be atoned for by sacrifice, intensifies the earlier word, stressing that persistent contempt for God, unrestrained, has passed beyond ordinary remedy.

debates.bearing: Either way the repetition marks Samuel's call as the restoration of God's reliable word and shows that God's warnings are sure, driving the reader to seek the atonement that only Christ can provide.

debates.question: What does it mean that Eli's iniquity will never be atoned for by sacrifice, verse 14?

views.label: A sentence of temporal judgment on the house
views.case: The oath concerns the removal of Eli's priestly line from its office and privilege in history; no ritual offering will avert the fall of the house, though it does not pronounce on the eternal state of every individual in it.

views.label: A warning about presuming on ritual while despising God
views.case: The very sacrifices Eli's sons defiled cannot now cover their sin; the verse exposes the emptiness of religion offered by hearts that hold God in contempt, pointing beyond ritual to the need for real repentance and a better atonement.

debates.bearing: Both readings warn against trusting religious ritual while despising God, and heighten the longing for the true and final atonement in Christ, which alone cleanses what no offering at Shiloh could.

debates.question: Did Samuel experience only an audible voice, or some accompanying vision as well?

views.label: An audible voice without visual theophany
views.case: The text repeatedly says only that the LORD called, describing no form or throne as Isaiah's vision does, which fits a boy not yet ready for a fuller visionary experience, verse 7's note that the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him.

views.label: A vision underlying the account
views.case: Verse 15 names what Samuel received as the vision, and verse 1 already frames the whole crisis as a scarcity of visions as much as words, suggesting some visual component accompanied the voice even though the narrator declines to describe it.

debates.bearing: Either way the chapter withholds the sensory details it does not consider essential, training the reader to focus on the reliability and content of the message rather than the drama of the experience, since fulfilled words, not described visions, are the test Deuteronomy 18 actually sets.

study.originalLanguages: Several further words reward attention beyond the chapter's frame of dabar, shama, and navi. The opening verse says the word of the LORD was yaqar, an adjective that means precious or costly as often as it means rare, so the line carries a double sense: God's speech was scarce because, in those days, it had become a treasure handled carelessly rather than sought after, precious and neglected at once. The same verse adds that chazon, vision, was not widespread, a term built on the verb to see and used elsewhere as virtually a synonym for prophecy itself, so the chapter's opening already frames the crisis as a double poverty, of hearing and of seeing. Eli's blindness is described with kahah, to grow dim or weak, a verb used elsewhere of eyesight failing with age, and the narrator lets that physical dimness stand as an unmistakable picture of the spiritual dimness of the whole era before turning to the boy who will restore Israel's hearing of God. The narrative repeats shakab, to lie down, again and again as Samuel returns to bed after each call, a small verb whose repetition becomes almost comic, underlining how ordinary and undramatic the surface of the scene remains even as something entirely uncommon unfolds beneath it. When God finally tells Samuel that the ears of all who hear this will tsalal, tingle or ring, the verb is genuinely rare, appearing in the whole Old Testament only here and twice more, both times introducing the announcement of an especially severe coming judgment, so its use here marks this word as belonging to the gravest class of prophetic pronouncement Israel's Scriptures record. God says He will kalah, complete or bring to an end, everything spoken against Eli's house, a verb of finishing rather than merely beginning, stressing that this sentence will run its full course rather than stopping partway. And the verdict itself turns on kaphar, to atone or cover, the very verbal root behind the Day of Atonement; to say Eli's house will never be kaphar by sacrifice or offering is to say that the ordinary machinery of Israel's entire sacrificial system has no answer for this particular sin, a genuinely severe claim given how much that system could normally cover. Finally, where verse 1 spoke of chazon, verse 15 shifts to a different word, mar'ah, a vision or a sight, for the very thing Samuel is now afraid to report, so Hebrew frames the identical revelatory event with two related but distinct terms across the chapter, one naming the category of experience Israel had lost, the other naming the specific thing Samuel had just been given.

typology.type: Samuel, the prophet raised up when God's word was scarce
typology.fulfillment: Moses had promised that God would raise up a prophet like himself from among the people, one through whom Israel must continue to hear God's voice on pain of judgment for ignoring him, Deuteronomy 18:15-18. Samuel is the first Old Testament figure the historical books explicitly confirm as filling that pattern, a prophet whose every word the LORD backs. Peter later applies the whole line of prophets beginning with Samuel directly to Jesus, telling the crowd at the temple that all the prophets from Samuel onward have proclaimed these days, and that the prophet Moses promised is this very Jesus, Acts 3:22-24, tracing the line from this bedroom in Shiloh to the resurrection itself.

typology.type: The listening servant who delivers God's word
typology.fulfillment: Samuel answers, speak, for Your servant is listening, and then delivers, without editing, a message he did not want to give. Jesus describes His own ministry in nearly identical terms, insisting that He does nothing on His own initiative but speaks only what the Father has taught Him, and that His Father's commandment is eternal life, so He speaks exactly what the Father has told Him to speak, John 8:28 and 12:49-50. Where Samuel's obedience cost him a hard, fearful conversation with a father figure he loved, Christ's perfect obedience to deliver the Father's word cost Him the cross, the same pattern of receiving and faithfully relaying carried to its full and costly extent.

typology.type: The judgment no sacrifice at Shiloh could atone
typology.fulfillment: The sentence on Eli's house explicitly closes off Israel's ordinary means of atonement, sacrifice and offering, leaving the household exposed with no ritual remedy available under the law as it then stood. Hebrews later diagnoses the same fundamental limitation in the entire sacrificial system, since the blood of bulls and goats can never actually take away sins, only cover them provisionally year after year, Hebrews 10:1-4. Christ's single offering succeeds precisely where Eli's inherited sacrifices could not, perfecting for all time those being sanctified, Hebrews 10:14, reaching sins that the old system, even at its best, could only postpone.

typology.type: The lamp of God not yet gone out
typology.fulfillment: The chapter opens in the last hours before the sanctuary lamp finally goes out, a small detail that becomes a fitting picture of the whole period, God's light in Israel burning low but not yet extinguished. John later takes up the image of light surviving darkness to describe Christ Himself, the true light that gives light to everyone, shining in the darkness, a darkness that has never overcome it, John 1:4-5. Where the lamp at Shiloh depended on human hands trimming its wick through the night, the light John describes cannot be put out by any darkness at all, since it is the very life of the eternal Word made flesh.

study.christ: When God tells Samuel that what is coming will make the ears of all who hear it tingle, He uses an idiom the Old Testament reserves for only its gravest announcements of coming judgment; the same rare phrase recurs when the LORD later warns of disaster coming on Jerusalem, 2 Kings 21:12, and Jeremiah 19:3. That such severe language first surfaces here, over the fall of one priestly family, teaches how seriously God regards the corruption of those entrusted with His worship, and it prepares the reader's ear for how much graver a hearing awaits anyone who neglects the far greater salvation later announced through God's own Son; the writer to the Hebrews asks directly how anyone will escape if they ignore a message first spoken through the Lord Himself and confirmed by those who heard Him, Hebrews 2:1-3, deliberately setting the stakes of gospel hearing above even this ancient warning. Samuel's recognition by all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, marks the outer edge of what a single prophet's authority could reach in his own lifetime, the whole tribal territory but no further. Christ's confirmation is not bounded even by that wide a horizon; Paul says that God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, Philippians 2:9-10, a recognition that dwarfs Samuel's national confirmation by including every creature that has ever lived. And where the chapter closes by noting that the LORD appeared repeatedly at Shiloh, revealing Himself to Samuel by His word, John's Gospel says that no one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known, John 1:18, the final and complete version of the revealing this chapter shows only beginning. Samuel heard a voice in the dark; the church has seen the Word made flesh in the full light of day.
study.god: One of the quieter but striking claims of this chapter is that God calls Samuel before Samuel knows Him at all, verse 7 states this almost bluntly, Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and yet the LORD had already called him three times by then. God does not wait for readiness, maturity, or even correct recognition before initiating relationship; He calls into existence a hearing where none previously existed, and only then, through Eli's patient coaching, gives Samuel the words to answer rightly. This is a striking picture of grace working ahead of understanding, the LORD pursuing a relationship the other party cannot yet properly name. The scene also holds together God's utter transcendence and His concrete nearness in one moment: this is the same LORD of Hosts enthroned over the ark, yet the text says plainly that He came and stood there in Samuel's sleeping quarters, calling as before, a nearness so immediate that a boy could reasonably, if mistakenly, assume it was his own elderly master's voice from another room. God's justice, too, is shown to be exact rather than vague; when He states the charge against Eli, He specifies the iniquity of which he knows, a particular, known failure to restrain sons whose sin he was fully aware of, not a general accusation of collective guilt against an entire household for sins no one could have anticipated or controlled. This precision matters: God does not punish blindly or by association alone, but names exactly where responsibility lay, Eli's knowledge and his failure to act on it. And His faithfulness reaches even into the specific promise that He continued to appear at Shiloh, because there He revealed Himself to Samuel by His word, showing that once God begins to restore His speech to a place or a person, He does not withdraw it again on a whim; having begun to speak, He keeps speaking, a small but real assurance of divine consistency across all of Samuel's subsequent ministry.

crossReferences.note: Moses promises a prophet like himself whom the people must heed, warning that God Himself will call to account anyone who refuses to listen to the words that prophet speaks in His name. Samuel becomes the first clear historical fulfillment of an ongoing line the passage opens, later completed in Christ.

Solomon declares at the temple's dedication that not one word has failed of all the good promise the LORD made through Moses, the same confidence this chapter first establishes about Samuel's own words, that the LORD lets none of them fall to the ground.

Isaiah receives his prophetic commission inside the sanctuary itself, seeing the LORD high and lifted up before answering, here am I, send me. Like Samuel's night call, the setting is close to God's own dwelling, and the prophet's own unworthiness is confronted before the commission is given.

Jeremiah, like Samuel a very young man, protests that he is only a boy and does not know how to speak, before the LORD overrules his hesitation and puts words directly in his mouth, the same pattern of an unready messenger given a message not his own.

The Lord God does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets, the same principle this chapter enacts when God discloses beforehand exactly what He is about to do to Eli's house rather than simply doing it without warning.

The LORD later warns that disaster coming on Jerusalem will make the ears of everyone who hears of it tingle, the identical rare idiom first used of Eli's house, showing this exact phrase reserved across Scripture for only the gravest announcements of judgment.

The prophet is told to announce disaster on Jerusalem so great that the ears of everyone who hears will tingle, the third and final Old Testament use of this rare idiom, each occurrence marking judgment of the most severe kind God pronounces.

Peter tells the crowd at the temple that all the prophets from Samuel and those after him have proclaimed these days, and that the prophet like Moses whom the people must hear is Jesus, explicitly naming Samuel as the start of the very line Christ completes.

God, who spoke long ago through the prophets in many portions and many ways, has in these last days spoken to us by His Son, gathering the entire line of partial, successive prophetic words that began with figures like Samuel into one final, complete word.

The writer asks how anyone will escape judgment if they neglect a salvation first announced by the Lord Himself, an argument built on the same logic this chapter assumes, that hearing God's word carries real consequence and cannot be safely ignored.

God exalted Jesus to the highest place and gave Him the name above every name, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess Him Lord, a confirmation and recognition that reaches every creature, far beyond the territory from Dan to Beersheba that first knew Samuel as a prophet.

study.oneStory: In the beginning, God simply spoke and the world came to be, and He walked and talked directly with the man and woman He had made; the scarcity of His word in Samuel's day is therefore not the normal condition of the world but a symptom of how far Israel's relationship with God had decayed under the judges, when everyone did what was right in his own eyes and, correspondingly, heard less and less from the One whose voice should have shaped their eyes in the first place. Amos will later describe an even worse version of this same famine, a time when God sends not famine of bread but of hearing the words of the LORD, so that people will wander from sea to sea seeking a word and not find one, Amos 8:11-12; this chapter shows the first small reversal of that trajectory, one boy given ears to hear before the famine becomes total. From this single restored voice, God rebuilds a nation's access to His speech: Samuel anoints Saul, and when Saul fails, anoints David, and through David's line the prophetic word keeps running, through court prophets and writing prophets alike, all of them tested by the very standard this chapter establishes, that a true word from God is a word that comes to pass. That entire long history of successive, partial prophetic speech is finally gathered up and completed when the Word Himself takes on flesh and dwells among us, no longer speaking occasionally in the night to a chosen few but living permanently among His people. And the trajectory that begins with a fading lamp in a dark sanctuary ends, in Scripture's last vision, with no lamp needed at all, because the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever, Revelation 22:5, the small flame Samuel lay beside becoming, at the very end of the story, the unclouded, undimmed presence of God Himself.

quiz.q: What was the spiritual condition of Israel at the start of the chapter?

options.text: The word of the LORD was rare and visions were scarce, a famine of God's speech.
options.note: Verse 1 sets the scene of spiritual silence that God is about to break.

options.text: Eli's eyesight had grown dim and he could barely see.
options.note: True, and a fitting picture of the age, but the broader point is the scarcity of God's word.

options.text: Israel was enjoying a golden age of prophecy and revelation.
options.note: The opposite; revelation was rare, which is why Samuel's call matters.

options.text: The nation had completely forgotten that God existed.
options.note: They still worshiped at Shiloh; the problem was God's word had grown rare, not total ignorance.

quiz.q: What did Eli teach Samuel to say when God called again?

options.text: Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening, a posture of ready obedience.
options.note: Verse 9; true hearing in Scripture leans toward obeying.

options.text: To answer the voice rather than keep running to Eli.
options.note: True in substance, but the exact words of humble, obedient listening are the point.

options.text: To demand that God prove who He was first.
options.note: Eli taught humble listening, not a demand for proof.

options.text: To ignore the voice until morning.
options.note: The opposite; Eli taught Samuel to answer and listen.

quiz.q: How is Samuel shown to be a true prophet?

options.text: The LORD was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground, so all Israel recognized him.
options.note: Verses 19 to 20; a true prophet's words come to pass, Deuteronomy 18.

options.text: He faithfully told Eli the whole hard message without hiding anything.
options.note: True and admirable, but the confirming mark is that his words all came true.

options.text: He performed many miracles before the people.
options.note: The text stresses reliable words, not a display of miracles.

options.text: He crowned himself king over Israel.
options.note: Samuel was a prophet and judge, never king.

quiz.q: How does Samuel's call point forward to Christ?

options.text: Samuel heads the line of prophets that ends in Christ, the Prophet like Moses and the Word of God we must hear.
options.note: Deuteronomy 18 and Acts 3 identify that prophet as Jesus, God's final Word.

options.text: He is a faithful servant who delivers only the word God gives him.
options.note: True, and like Christ, but it omits that Jesus is the Prophet and Word Samuel anticipates.

options.text: He shows that God speaks only to children.
options.note: God's initiative to a boy is striking, but the point is not that God speaks only to children.

options.text: He has no connection to Christ.
options.note: Samuel begins the prophetic line fulfilled in Jesus.

quiz.q: What does the chapter reveal about God?

options.text: He takes the initiative to speak, patiently calling, and He keeps both His word of judgment and His faithfulness to His people.
options.note: God calls Samuel first, calls repeatedly, confirms His judgment, and restores His word to Israel.

options.text: He is a God who speaks and reveals Himself to His servants.
options.note: True, but only part of the fuller picture of His initiative, patience, justice, and faithfulness.

options.text: He speaks only through visible signs and never by His word.
options.note: The chapter centers precisely on God speaking by His word.

options.text: He had abandoned Israel and no longer cared to speak.
options.note: The whole point is that God breaks the silence and speaks again.

questions: God's word had grown rare in Israel, yet He spoke to a boy who was ready to listen. Is your life quiet enough, and your heart ready enough, to hear from God through His word?
Samuel answered, Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening. What would change if you came to Scripture and prayer each day with that same posture of ready obedience?
Samuel was afraid to tell Eli the hard message but told him everything. Where might God be calling you to speak a difficult but true word in love, rather than hiding it?
Eli responded to a hard word with, He is the LORD; let Him do what is good in His eyes. How can you learn to submit to God's will even when it is painful?
God let none of Samuel's words fall to the ground. How does the trustworthiness of God's word give you confidence to build your life on it?

translationNotes.note: Before the lamp of God had gone out places the scene in the last of the night; the sanctuary lamp burned until morning, a fitting image for a dim spiritual age.
His sons blasphemed God follows the Septuagint; the Hebrew reads made themselves contemptible, but the sense of grave, unrestrained sin stands either way.
From Dan to Beersheba is a set expression for the whole land, from its northern to its southern edge, marking that all Israel recognized Samuel as a prophet.
